Al Grey’s trombone sound is immediately recognizable in the world of jazz.

Born in 1925, he first played trombone in a Navy band. Early career highlights included work with Lionel Hampton, Benny Carter and Dizzy Gillespie. When a Basie trombone player became ill, Al stepped in and ended up playing with the orchestra from 1957-61 and 1964-77. His outstanding use of the plunger mute led to a Fred Astaire choreographed dance around one of his Basie solos. Al is a featured player at numerous festivals and jazz parties and directs Lionel Hampton’s Golden Men of Jazz.
Al was interviewed in Scottsdale, Arizona on March 3, 1995 by Dr. Michael Woods.

Okay these are some professionally taped video interviews with some of today’s greatest jazz musicians. We’re taping these interviews for Hamilton College to create an archive of jazz history and of oral culture and some of the recollections of our greatest musicians and what we consider cultural assets in this country. I’m interviewing Al Grey right now and we’re just going to talk a little bit about some of the things that were effective in his life and some of his times with Count Basie and with Joe Williams. First of all, it’s a real pleasure to have you, an honor.
What a great interviewer. I’ll have a moment to say hi out there to the jazz world.
Yes. You told me of some of the places and people that you performed with before you met Count Basie. Start us there and bring us into your time with Count Basie.
